title: Germany and the Allied Industrial Base
subtitle: What to secure, build, source from partners, and deploy

inlines.v: Germany's distinctive role in the Allied Industrial Base is as its integrated equipment maker. It holds a role in all
strategic compacts and a core seat in

economies count it as their best-placed trusted partner somewhere in the chain. Allies rely on it as their largest holder of vehicle supply and, on mixed trade codes, of drivetrain, grid-equipment and wind-part supply. Its exposure lies in imported fuel, minerals it does not mine, refined rare earths and battery cells, where

of cell and pack imports. Its industrial effort should keep EV making, drivetrains and grid equipment at the frontier, and catch up in battery cells and components, where its own need is high. For minerals it should depend deliberately on trusted producers, and development cooperation can add drivetrain and battery capacity with developing partners. At home, storage, EVs and solar need to be deployed faster. The high fence belongs around fuel supply, the rare-earth chain, battery control software and transformer steel.

blocks.title: What Germany needs to deploy faster
blocks.alt: Bar chart of Germany's deployment need by technology, marking Accelerate and Watch and the main driver of each.

inlines.v: Deployment need by technology, with the largest of its measures: demand adequacy, the gap to national targets, or system need. Review cases, which rest on a single indicator of low confidence, are shown apart in grey and are not deployment priorities.
Wind power and grid networks sit just below the bar (

), so a small change in the data would make them Accelerate. High deployment priority does not imply high manufacturing priority. Germany is catching up in batteries, but storage should not wait: equipment should come from whichever trusted supplier is ready, with the fence on battery control software. Clean hydrogen reads Accelerate on a single indicator of low confidence, so it is a review case.

That is little recorded industrial-policy attention; it says nothing about actual stocks, so stocks and contracts should be tested against the rebuild time. Second, the Preserve calls in drivetrains and EV making get less recorded attention than they need. Finally, protection is highest on wafers and PV cells and on grid components, both Watch steps, and on solar generally (
at deployment); that effort should shift toward deployment. The battery-recycling row rests on an export anchor of scrap: a data flag, not a call for new support.

blocks.text: 3. Catch up across the battery chain, and fence its control software

inlines.v: Tie production incentives, first-of-a-kind finance and workforce and supplier development to benchmarks, with sunsets, in cells, components and materials refining. Build at home where the base is established and with allied partners for the rest. Require certified, trusted battery firmware, and replace untrusted control in the installed base on a deadline.

blocks.text: 4. Keep vehicles, drivetrains and grid equipment at the frontier

inlines.v: Back next-generation R&D, workforce and supplier development and finance for expansion, tied to benchmarks under which support per unit falls. Keep the gate open to allied investment and import competition, with trade remedies only where unfair competition threatens the base. Allies rely on this supply, so reliability is part of the case.

blocks.text: 5. Build trusted drivetrain and battery capacity with developing partners

inlines.v: , which rests on German need alone: its Preserve design sets no partner finance. The objective is both an additional trusted supplier and a durable capability in the partner economy.

blocks.text: 6. Accelerate storage, EVs and solar while keeping sourcing open

inlines.v: Deploy faster through infrastructure, permitting and procurement, buying commodity hardware competitively with security conditions on connected equipment. Shift effort from protecting wafers, cells and grid components to deployment.
Every number comes from the Country page data of the Allied Industrial Base Explorer (the data release of
) and from the Allied Industrial Base analysis. Each technology is split into supply-chain stages from extraction to recycling, and each step gets a strategic choice by fixed rules applied in order:
Secure where an acute vulnerability is measured;
at deployment, Accelerate where deployment need reaches
Watch where the step is a large, commoditized yard;
Preserve where Competitive Position is in the top quarter (
Catch Up where the value is high, the position is not, and a capability anchor is corroborated by other evidence;
Partner where supply-chain need is high but there is neither a top-quarter position nor, for a high-value step, a credible pathway;

Named layers inside a step, such as control software or magnets, take their own choice, and a step whose parts sit behind different fences is mixed. A value that rests on market size alone is capped just under the bar. Observed policy never decides a choice. The high fence (Secure) protects what cannot be allowed to fail; the medium fence covers capabilities worth building, keeping or sourcing deliberately and deployment to accelerate; the low fence (Watch) leaves a step open to competitive purchase.

Some calls rest on low confidence, an engine review flag, a thin capability anchor, a known data artifact or, at deployment, a single indicator of low confidence. They stay on the map but never enter the Bottom line, the Agenda, the policy table or a headline mark.

Competitive Position ranks Germany among economies that already supply a step, so a zero means no measurable position. Partner lists name where allied capacity sits, which can include trading hubs, not who owns it.

A pair joins a German step with a strategic reason for more allied capacity, Germany's own need or the allied gap alone, and a developing economy whose same step is a credible Catch Up inside the AIB trust screen. On a step whose data describe different products, the partner's anchor must measure the product the need is about. A partner that already hosts the step's new capacity in the AIB, or Preserves it, is a commercial case. Aid comes from the OECD Creditor Reporting System and covers energy, industry and mining purpose codes only; Components and Assembly share codes, no code funds recycling, and many codes name a stage rather than a technology. A constraint on a partner is named only where the data observe its input. Export-credit finance is reported apart and never counted as aid, and the direct investment position is economy-wide. The full list of pairs is in the development-partnership export.
